821.event_title: Germany breaks the Nazi-Soviet Pact and invades the Soviet Union
821.place: Moscow and the western Soviet Union
821.event: On 23 August 1939 Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union signed a ten-year non-aggression pact in Moscow, negotiated by their foreign ministers Joachim von Ribbentrop and Vyacheslav Molotov, with a secret protocol dividing eastern Europe into spheres of influence. Hitler regarded the pact as a temporary tactical move, and in July 1940 he decided to attack the Soviet Union within the following year. On 22 June 1941 more than three million German soldiers invaded the Soviet Union, ending the pact after less than two years.
821.explanation: The pact gave each side what it wanted for a time, but for Germany it was only a platform from which to prepare the attack it had always intended.
821.tie_back: The kural compares the friendship of those who are outwardly close but not one at heart to an anvil, a seeming support that is really the base on which you will be struck when the moment comes, and the pact served Germany in exactly that way.
821._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the anvil image: an outward agreement used as the base for a planned strike at the right time.

822.event_title: Warwick the Kingmaker turns against Edward IV
822.event: Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick, Edward IV's cousin, had been the chief supporter who helped make him king in 1461. After quarrels over Edward's marriage to Elizabeth Woodville and his growing independence, Warwick rebelled, fled to France in 1470, and was reconciled there with his former enemy Margaret of Anjou, wife of the Lancastrian king Henry VI. Returning to England in September 1470, he drove Edward into exile and put Henry VI back on the throne, but Edward returned and Warwick was killed at the Battle of Barnet in April 1471.
822.explanation: Warwick moved from kinsman and kingmaker to enemy as his own influence rose and fell, showing how little a kin-like bond meant when interests changed.
822.tie_back: The kural says the friendship of those who seem like your own people but are not will shift with what they can gain, and Warwick, Edward's own cousin and chief ally, changed sides when his standing at court declined.
822._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of shifting loyalty within the family circle, though Warwick was a real kinsman rather than one who only resembled kin.

823.event_title: Seneca's teaching fails to make Nero good
823.event: The Stoic philosopher Seneca became tutor to the young Nero in 49 CE and, after Nero became emperor in 54, served as one of his chief advisers. Nero relied less and less on Seneca's counsel, and around 62 Seneca withdrew from public life and devoted himself to writing philosophy. In 65, after Seneca's enemies accused him of a part in the Pisonian conspiracy against Nero, the emperor ordered his death.
823.explanation: Years of instruction by one of Rome's leading moral philosophers did not make Nero a good ruler, and in the end he turned against his own teacher.
823.tie_back: The kural says that even after studying many good books, those who lack inner nobility rarely become truly good-hearted toward you, and Nero, schooled by Seneca himself, ended by condemning him.
823._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit for learning that fails to change the heart, though the kural speaks of a hostile person's own reading, and Seneca's involvement in the conspiracy is uncertain.

824.event_title: An Lushan, the emperor's favourite, rebels against the Tang
824.event: An Lushan, a general of Sogdian and Turkish origin, rose in the 740s to command all three northeastern military regions, with about 160,000 troops, and on his frequent visits to the capital became a personal favourite of Emperor Xuanzong and his consort Yang Guifei. Toward the end of 755, claiming a secret order from the emperor to remove the chief minister Yang Guozhong, he marched his army on the capital. He took Luoyang, proclaimed himself emperor in 756 and captured Chang'an, forcing Xuanzong to flee to Sichuan.
824.explanation: The general who had won the emperor's warm personal favour became the leader of a rebellion that shook the Tang dynasty for eight years.
824.tie_back: The kural warns against deceivers whose faces smile sweetly while their hearts are bitter, and An Lushan rose as a court favourite before turning his army against the emperor who had trusted him.
824._accuracy_note: A strong fit for a pleasant favourite who became an enemy, though the sources describe his court favour and rebellion rather than documenting a deliberate inner hostility while he was in favour.

825.event_title: Shivaji escapes from Aurangzeb's detention at Agra
825.event: Under the Treaty of Purandar, made after his defeat by the Mughal general Jai Singh, the Maratha leader Shivaji agreed to visit the court of Emperor Aurangzeb, and he arrived at Agra in May 1666 with Jai Singh's promise that he would be allowed to return home safely. The audience went badly, and Shivaji was kept under guard rather than allowed to leave. Later that year he escaped with his son Sambhaji, reached his own territory again and resumed his struggle against the Mughals.
825.explanation: Shivaji learned that the assurances given in a treaty with an opponent counted for little once he was in that opponent's power.
825.tie_back: The kural says the words of those who are not one with you in heart should not be relied on in any matter, and Shivaji's trust in the promises of safe conduct ended in detention at Agra.
825._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of the danger of relying on an opponent's assurances, though the promise of safe return came from Jai Singh rather than Aurangzeb himself.

826.event_title: Menelik II rejects Italy's reading of the Treaty of Wuchale
826.event: In 1889 Emperor Menelik II of Ethiopia signed a treaty of friendship with Italy, known as the Treaty of Wuchale (Wichale). Article 17 in the Amharic text allowed Ethiopia to use Italy's good offices in dealing with other powers, while the Italian text made this obligatory, and Italy used its version to proclaim a protectorate over Ethiopia. Menelik rejected the claim in 1890, denounced the whole treaty in 1893, and after his victory at Adwa in 1896 Italy accepted the treaty's annulment and recognised Ethiopia's independence.
826.explanation: A treaty presented as friendship concealed a claim to control, and Menelik saw through it and refused to accept it.
826.tie_back: The kural says that even when enemies speak good words as if they were friends, their real nature is soon seen, and the friendly treaty's hidden meaning was quickly recognised and repudiated by Menelik.
826._accuracy_note: A strong fit: an apparently friendly agreement whose hostile meaning was detected and rejected, though it took months rather than moments.

827.event_title: Japan's envoys keep negotiating in Washington as the Pearl Harbor fleet sails
827.place: Washington, D.C., and Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, United States
827.event: Through late 1941 Ambassador Kichisaburo Nomura and special envoy Saburo Kurusu held talks in Washington with Secretary of State Cordell Hull, holding out hope of a negotiated settlement. On 26 November 1941 a Japanese carrier fleet secretly left the Kuril Islands for Hawaii while the talks continued. On 7 December the envoys reached Hull's office with Japan's reply shortly after 2 p.m. Washington time, after the attack on Pearl Harbor had already begun.
827.explanation: Courteous diplomacy continued in Washington while a striking force was already on its way, so the talks gave no warning of what was coming.
827.tie_back: The kural says a foe's humble, bowing speech should not be trusted, just as a bow bends only to do harm, and the polite negotiations ran side by side with the preparation of the attack.
827._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of courteous words masking harm, though the envoys themselves were not told of the attack and the late delivery of the note was caused by decoding delays.

828.event_title: The Great Seal gift hides a Soviet listening device
828.place: U.S. ambassador's residence, Moscow, Soviet Union
828.event: On 4 August 1945 a group of Soviet schoolchildren presented a hand-carved wooden replica of the Great Seal of the United States to the American ambassador, Averell Harriman, as a gesture of friendship between wartime allies. The carving hung in the ambassador's residence until 1952, when U.S. security officers discovered a hidden passive listening device, later called The Thing, inside it. In May 1960 Ambassador Henry Cabot Lodge Jr. displayed the seal at the United Nations Security Council to show how it had been used for spying.
828.explanation: A gift offered in friendship, by children and in a time of alliance, turned out to conceal an instrument used against the recipient.
828.tie_back: The kural says a weapon may lie hidden even in hands joined in worship, and the friendly gift of the Great Seal concealed a device for spying on the very people it honoured.
828._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural: a token of friendship that literally hid the means of harm.

829.event_title: Cesare Borgia's reconciliation with his captains at Senigallia
829.event: In October 1502 several of Cesare Borgia's own condottieri met at Magione and conspired against him, and over the following weeks they negotiated a reconciliation and returned to his service. At the end of December, Vitellozzo Vitelli, Oliverotto da Fermo and two members of the Orsini family met Borgia at Senigallia, which they had just taken in his name. Borgia separated them from their troops, arrested them, and had them put to death, an episode described by Machiavelli, who was then an envoy at Borgia's side.
829.explanation: Both sides made a show of renewed friendship while neither trusted the other, and the reconciliation ended in Borgia's sudden blow.
829.tie_back: The kural describes those who make a great show of friendship while secretly despising you, and advises answering with outward cordiality while letting the bond die within, which is how Borgia treated the captains who had plotted against him.
829._accuracy_note: A strong case of pretence answered with pretence, but Borgia's ruthless ending goes far beyond the kural's advice to let such a friendship quietly die.

830.event_title: Alexander I's alliance with Napoleon after Tilsit
830.place: Tilsit, East Prussia (now Sovetsk, Russia), and Russia
830.event: After Russia's defeat at Friedland, Tsar Alexander I met Napoleon on a raft in the Neman River, and in July 1807 the Treaty of Tilsit made Russia France's ally and committed it to Napoleon's Continental Blockade against British trade. Russia's economy depended heavily on British trade, and its support for the blockade was half-hearted. On 31 December 1810 Alexander issued a decree reopening Russian ports to neutral shipping, which in effect readmitted British trade, and in June 1812 Napoleon invaded Russia.
830.explanation: An alliance forced on Alexander by defeat was kept up in public for a time and then allowed to lapse once Russia was ready to stand on its own.
830.tie_back: The kural says that when an enemy must for a time be treated as a friend, one should be friendly in face, keep friendship out of the heart, and let it go when one can, which is the course the Tilsit alliance followed.
830._accuracy_note: A close fit for an alliance of necessity kept outwardly and abandoned when possible, though Alexander's private feelings at Tilsit are not directly documented in these sources.
